name: Crisis Language Goes to a Person
title: Crisis Language Goes to a Person
answer: Any tool students use to discuss feelings or health must route crisis language to a trained adult immediately instead of trying to handle it itself. This is the most important safety rule in the book's wellbeing, behavior, attendance, and safety chapter, because a delayed or missed alert can leave a student in danger without help.

sections.body: This idea sets a single non negotiable rule for every tool students might use to talk about their feelings or health: when a student writes something that suggests self harm, suicide, abuse, or danger, the tool must alert a trained adult right away rather than attempt its own response. The rule covers wellness chatbots, health question tools, and any chat tool students can access, so the same standard applies across the school. The problem it solves is the gap between a tool that seems supportive and a tool that is actually safe when risk is imminent. Many products are not built for that moment, and schools cannot assume otherwise. Routing crisis language to a person keeps the response with someone trained to act.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the rule becomes a routine before any student touches the tool. Staff type phrases that suggest self harm or danger and then confirm that alerts reach the right person quickly, including after school hours and on weekends. The same testing is repeated after any update to the tool, since a change can break the routing. Students are also told about the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which they can call or text at any time. The text does not give separate steps by grade band, so the practice applies the same way across year groups.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as practice backed by review evidence rather than a single trial. A review of 39 mental health chatbots for young people found that few had adequate safety features for situations of imminent risk, and most studies ignored ethical questions entirely (Park et al., 2025). A scoping review of AI in schools found that risks to students' psychological wellbeing, including emotional disconnection and isolation, were among the main concerns (Tao et al., 2026). Together these findings support the book's warning that schools cannot assume a tool handles crises well.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by the rule itself: the tool must not try to respond to crisis language on its own, and the alert must go to a trained adult immediately. Testing before use, after hours and weekend checks, and retesting after every update are the safeguards the text requires. The decisions that stay with people are the routing choices, who receives the alert, and how quickly staff respond, none of which the tool can own. The text also notes that many tools fall short on imminent risk and that ethical questions are often ignored, so adoption without verification is the main risk. Nothing here is legal advice, and the practice described is operational rather than a compliance standard.
